gap: B makes the marker run the only cue to heading level — all six levels are set at an identical 30px cap height and identical 6px word stem, zero size or weight differentiation from H1 to H6 — and then draws that run at a 3px stem, half the word's mass, so telling `#####` from `######` at a glance takes a deliberate second look where A's heavier run resolves the count immediately.
gapTheirs: A draws the `#` runs at the same stroke mass as the heading word — 5px stems vs B's 3px, ~48% more ink area per glyph measured at each image's own 50%-of-peak threshold — and at this size A's two crossbars fuse (scanlines y=404 through y=416 are solid across the glyph), closing the counters so `######` renders as a 155px slab rather than six ticks; setting the grey aside, the gutter carries more visual weight than the three-word heading beside it, which is the opposite of what a hanging marker is for.
verdict: Both put the words on one column; only B puts them on a grid. A's staircase steps 26/26/25/26/25px instead of a clean cell and its baselines fall 74/73/73/73/73 instead of a metronomic 74, so A's H6 ink lands at x=43 where the cell arithmetic (224 − 7×26) says 41–42 — it stops two pixels short of the container edge it was supposed to reach, and the left staircase wobbles on two of six rows. Worse, A's hash runs are drawn at nearly the word's own weight with their counters filled in, so by H5 the eye reads the gutter first and the heading second; you have built a second column of content, not a margin. B's flaw is that it gives you no type-size hierarchy at all and then whispers the one cue that carries it — but a writer will take a level they must count over a gutter that shouts, and B's 26px step and 74px baseline never move under the cursor.

states.name: blocks
states.gap: B's cell advance is 26.1px vs A's 25.6px (~2% larger type), so the same 20-character line runs to x731 instead of x722 — right margin 49px vs 58px, ~16% less trailing air before the container edge — while line-height stays 74px = 2.83 cells vs A's 2.85, a fractionally tighter page in the same 780×620 viewport.
states.gapTheirs: A sets the `######` run in the heading's own bold face at the same stem weight as the words, so at 25.6px pitch the bold hashes collide — measured inter-glyph gaps of 0,1,0,1,1px, with hashes 1-2 and 3-4 fused into solid 50px-wide runs (x42..91, x93..142). The six-hash gutter reads as one 152px slab of markup, uncountable at a glance; B's regular-weight run has uniform 1px gaps across all six.
states.verdict: Strip the marker greys out of the argument, as instructed, and these two are the same layout to within two pixels: same body column at x222, same seven-cell hang to x40, same `>`/`-`/`1.` sitting on the column and shoving their words in, no rule beside the quote in either. What is left is that A bolds its hash run to match the heading, and the stems touch — you get a solid bar of punctuation before you get the word, and you cannot count six of anything in it. B's markers stay at text weight with a clean 1px rhythm, which is the only reason to prefer it; it buys that with 2% larger type crowding 9px closer to the right rail. This is a coin-flip won on one detail, not a design gap.
secondary: Both: H6 is body-size bold only — no size step, so heading level is legible only by counting hashes in the gutter
Both: quote gets no rule and no indent of its own; `>` on the body column pushes the words 2 cells in, identical treatment to `-`
Both: bullet `-` ink starts 2-3px right of the body column ('B' at x225, '-' at x227/228) — hyphen bearing, not a misalignment
Marker greyness excluded per brief (A markers 205 = same as text; B markers 128 against 204 text)
